plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) months 2–6: what to expect after the first month, told by experience (appetite and food noise, how stomach side effects tend to change, the shape of average weight change, hair shedding, the birth-control note around dose increases, injection-site reactions) using only the US labels and SURMOUNT-1
plan.angle:
Tirzepatide months 2–6: what the US labels and SURMOUNT-1 say about the months after the first one. The title leads with 'Tirzepatide' (e.g. 'Tirzepatide After Month 1: What Months 2–6 Can Look Like'). Brand names appear only with their own label's data, and Mounjaro figures only if labelled as type 2 diabetes trials. Thumbnail text: 'AFTER MONTH 1' or 'MONTHS 2–6: WHAT CHANGES', with one calm labelled character and no body imagery.

Chapters stay organised by experience:
(1) Appetite: label mechanism (reduced appetite and food intake). 'Food noise' is framed as a viewer term, with no promise it stays quiet.
(2) Stomach side effects: 'mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'. Pooled nausea rates name the Zepbound weight-management trial pool vs placebo.
(3) Weight: SURMOUNT-1 average curve shape in words, for tirzepatide vs placebo, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes, over 72 weeks. Only figures stated in text, never read off the graph. Framed as averages, not predictions, pointing to the Plateau and How Long videos.
(4) Hair shedding: 5.4% vs 0.9% (women 7.1%, men 0.5%) in the Zepbound weight trials, with a hedged link to faster weight loss. See a doctor if it's patchy or lasts.
(5) ORAL hormonal contraceptives only: tirzepatide may make them less effective for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase. Ask your prescriber about non-oral or backup options. Other methods are not mentioned as affected.
(6) Injection-site reactions: 6–8% vs about 2% on placebo. Rotation tip credited to the Mounjaro/Zepbound IFU at its own URL.
(7) Questions for your prescriber, plus protein (kidney caveat) and gentle strength training, marked 'recommended'.

Safety: emergency card for severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting (get help right away), followed by the scoped don't-stop/change line. Low-blood-sugar caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea. No dose numbers, no titration and no week-by-week dosing calendar. Include 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line.
plan.why:
Playbook queue #5 and the planned sequel to First Month. It's a broad, searched what-to-expect question that can be verified fully from the US labels and NEJM, and it doesn't repeat either dropped topic or today's Shorts. | fact-check: This is a good evergreen sequel with real search demand, and it fits the channel focus. The guardrails are mostly right: no dose numbers, organised by experience, an emergency card, a hypoglycaemia caveat and scoped trial populations. It needs a few accuracy and packaging fixes first.

1) BIRTH CONTROL SCOPE: the Zepbound/Mounjaro label note covers ORAL hormonal contraceptives only, not all birth control. Tirzepatide's delayed stomach emptying may reduce how well oral contraceptives work. The label advises switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method, for 4 weeks after starting and for 4 weeks after each dose increase. The chapter must say 'oral' every time, on screen and in narration. It must not imply that IUDs, implants, injections, patches or rings are affected. It must not present slower stomach emptying as the proven cause; keep the label's 'may'. Keep 'ask your prescriber about backup options'.

2) TITLE / BRAND SCOPE: the working title names only Mounjaro, but most of the data (pooled nausea, hair loss 5.4% vs 0.9%, injection-site rates, SURMOUNT-1) comes from the Zepbound label and obesity trials. Mounjaro is approved for type 2 diabetes. Lead with 'Tirzepatide'. If a brand appears, use both, or tie each number to its own label. Because the title keyword names Mounjaro, the injection-site-rotation tip must cite Mounjaro's own IFU at its own URL. Never use the PI page or a PI anchor.

3) MONTHS 2–6 FRAMING: the US labels give no month-by-month data. The weight chapter may describe the shape of SURMOUNT-1's average curve for both arms (tirzepatide doses vs placebo; adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes; 72 weeks). Do not give figures read off the graph, even labelled 'about'. Use only timepoints the paper or label states in text. Otherwise describe the shape in words ('kept going down over months, not weeks, then levelled off later in the 72-week trial'). 'Months 2–6' lines up with the dose-escalation period, so never name which dose or which week a viewer will be on.

4) THUMBNAIL: 'MONTH 3 ALREADY?' suggests a specific month-3 event the video doesn't deliver. Use text that matches the scope, e.g. 'MONTHS 2–6: WHAT CHANGES' or 'AFTER MONTH 1'. Keep one calm labelled character and no body imagery.

5) 'Food noise' is not label wording. Present it as a viewer term. Explain the appetite mechanism in label terms (reduced appetite and food intake), with no promise that it stays quiet.

6) The hair loss figures (5.4% vs 0.9%; women 7.1%, men 0.5%) come from the Zepbound weight-management trials pool. Name that pool. Phrase the link to faster weight loss with the label's hedge ('may'). The nausea-per-dose stat must name its pool: Zepbound weight-management trials, all of whom had obesity or overweight with a weight-related condition. Never compare Mounjaro type 2 diabetes rates with Zepbound rates as if they came from a head-to-head trial.

7) Emergency card: severe stomach pain that won't go away, 'with or without vomiting', 'right away', then 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Protein needs a kidney-disease caveat. Strength training should be started gently and cleared with a clinician where relevant.

8) Publisher: the 'video I'd watch next' line needs a verified Side Effects video URL in the post notes. Never use the channel home page.

package.description:
Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting? Get medical help right away. Swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing? Get medical help right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. On insulin or a sulfonylurea? Ask your prescriber about low blood sugar.

At week 72 in SURMOUNT-1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes), average weight was 15–20.9% lower on tirzepatide, depending on dose, vs 3.1% on placebo.

script.hook_pattern: Visceral 'you' scenario plus open loop: sentence 1 names tirzepatide and the title question. The short answer lands by 15 s and a concrete nausea number by 30 s. A one-sentence open loop about the gap between women and men in hair loss pays off in the hair chapter.

scenes.narration: You're past your first month on tirzepatide, so what do months two to six look like?
scenes.on_screen_text: Tirzepatide: what do months 2–6 look like?
scenes.retention_device: Hook: the drug and the viewer's exact question in sentence 1

scenes.narration: Short answer: in the Zepbound label's trials, stomach side effects happened mostly during dose escalation, and decreased over time.
And in the main weight trial, average weight kept going down over months, not weeks, then levelled off later in the 72-week trial.
scenes.retention_device: Second half of the answer, about the shape of the weight curve

scenes.narration: Here's one number up front. In the Zepbound weight-management trials, nausea was reported by 25 to 29 percent of people on tirzepatide, depending on dose, versus 8 percent on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Nausea: tirzepatide vs placebo, Zepbound weight trials
visual.stock_query: calm character beside big stat card

scenes.narration: Flip that around. Roughly 7 in 10 people on tirzepatide in those trials didn't report nausea at all.

scenes.narration: Picture Dana, 47. She's imaginary, but her questions might sound familiar.

visual.stock_query: friendly woman at kitchen table, thoughtful

scenes.narration: She's five weeks in. The first-month jitters have faded, but fresh questions keep arriving. Will the quiet around food last? Will the nausea come back? Why is the scale slower some weeks?

items: Will the quiet around food last?

scenes.retention_device: Lists the questions the video will answer

scenes.narration: If you feel that same mix of hope and worry, you're not alone. It's a very human place to be.
scenes.retention_device: Names the feeling and validates it

scenes.narration: And stay for the hair chapter. There's a gap between women and men that rarely gets mentioned.
scenes.on_screen_text: Hair: a gap between women and men
scenes.retention_device: Open loop (one sentence), paid off in the hair chapter

scenes.narration: One honest note first. The US labels don't give a month-by-month calendar. So we'll go by the evidence: the Zepbound and Mounjaro labels and the big SURMOUNT-1 trial.
scenes.retention_device: Roadmap of the chapters, with honest framing

scenes.narration: First question: will the quiet around food last?
scenes.on_screen_text: Will the quiet around food last?

visual.stock_query: chapter card, quiet fridge at night

scenes.narration: You might call it food noise: that running chatter about the next snack. It's a term viewers use, not one the label uses.

visual.stock_query: chattering snack bubbles around head at night

scenes.retention_device: A lived moment the viewer recognises

scenes.narration: Here's what the Zepbound label does say. GLP-1 is a natural regulator of appetite and calorie intake. Receptors for both GIP and GLP-1 are found in brain areas involved in appetite, and animal studies show tirzepatide reaches and activates those areas.
The label also says tirzepatide slows how fast the stomach empties. That delay is largest after the first dose and lessens over time, so it's one measured effect, not the whole story of appetite.
Here's the honest part. Nothing in the label promises that food noise stays quiet for good.

visual.myth: Food noise stays gone for good
visual.fact: The label makes no such promise
visual.stock_query: myth versus fact cards, calm mascot

scenes.narration: Some weeks, Dana's appetite feels turned way down. Other weeks, on a stressful day, the old cravings knock again.

visual.stock_query: woman ignoring knocking snack at door

scenes.narration: That isn't a willpower failure. It's a body and a brain, not a machine, and appetite can vary from week to week.
Having a plan for the louder weeks helps, and we'll build one in the last chapter. First, the stomach.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: promises a later payoff, then a chapter change

scenes.narration: Does the nausea come back when the dose goes up?
Here's what the label found. In the trials, nausea, diarrhea and vomiting happened mostly during dose escalation, and decreased over time.

visual.stock_query: stomach on staircase, calmer at top

scenes.narration: The SURMOUNT-1 paper said something similar. The most common side effects were stomach-related, mostly mild to moderate, and they happened primarily during dose escalation.

visual.quote: The most common adverse events with tirzepatide were gastrointestinal, and most were mild to moderate in severity, occurring primarily during dose escalation.
visual.attribution: SURMOUNT-1, New England Journal of Medicine, 2022

scenes.retention_device: A second source that confirms the first

scenes.narration: Here's why that matters for these months. Months two to six often include dose increases, on whatever schedule your prescriber sets.

visual.stock_query: friendly doctor with calendar, no numbers

scenes.retention_device: Links the evidence to the viewer's timeline

scenes.narration: So a queasy few days after a step up fits the pattern the trials saw. It doesn't automatically mean something's wrong, but it's worth mentioning to your prescriber.
scenes.on_screen_text: Queasy after a step up? Tell them

visual.stock_query: woman sipping tea, phoning clinic calmly

scenes.narration: How many people stopped because of side effects? In SURMOUNT-1, on tirzepatide, the low end was four point three percent. The high end was seven point one percent, depending on dose.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for side effects on tirzepatide, SURMOUNT-1

scenes.narration: On placebo, it was two point six percent, over the same 72 weeks. So more than 9 in 10 people on tirzepatide didn't stop because of side effects.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for side effects on placebo, 72 weeks
visual.stock_query: two bars side by side, calm

scenes.narration: One more label point. Kidney problems have been reported, mostly in people who got dehydrated from nausea, vomiting or diarrhea.

visual.stock_query: thirsty cartoon kidneys with water glass

scenes.narration: So sip fluids through a rough patch, and tell your prescriber if you can't keep fluids down.
One sign is never wait-and-see. If you have severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, get medical help right away.

visual.stock_query: calm neutral mascot with alert sign

So that's what tends to change. Next, what actually helps you through it.

scenes.narration: So what can make months two to six easier?
Start with the label. Zepbound is meant to be used alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity. The medicine is one part of the plan.
A helpful habit: build meals around protein, which may help you hold on to muscle while you lose weight. If you have kidney disease, ask your doctor before you increase protein.
Gentle strength training, started slowly, can help too. If you have a heart, joint or other health condition, clear it with your clinician first.
On queasy weeks, smaller meals, eating slowly and stopping when you're full may make things easier.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the plan promised in chapter 1

Back to Dana. Five weeks in, she wanted to know what's next. Here's what the evidence gives her.

In the Zepbound label's trials, stomach side effects happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time. In SURMOUNT-1, average weight on tirzepatide kept falling over months, then levelled off later in the 72 weeks.
In the Zepbound weight-management trials, hair loss was more common on tirzepatide than on placebo, and among people on tirzepatide, more common in women than in men.
scenes.on_screen_text: Hair loss on tirzepatide: more common in women

scenes.narration: If you use oral birth control, ask about backup for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase. And change your injection spot each week.
Appetite may get louder some weeks. That's a body, not a failure, and protein plus gentle strength work can support you along the way.
This is part of our series on your first months with tirzepatide. Subscribe, and the next part will find you.

factcheck.summary:
I checked the script against the Zepbound label (current DailyMed version, revised 8/2026), the SURMOUNT-1 abstract, and the American Academy of Dermatology shedding page. All the numbers I could open match the sources, and each keeps its drug, comparison group, population and timeframe:
- Nausea: 25, 29 and 28% by dose vs 8% on placebo, so "~7 in 10" with no nausea holds.
- Injection-site reactions: 6, 8 and 8% vs 2% on placebo.
- Hair loss by sex on tirzepatide: 7.1% in women vs 0.5% in men.
- SURMOUNT-1: 2,539 adults; average weight 15.0 to 20.9% lower vs 3.1% on placebo.
- Stomach side effects came mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time.
- The oral birth control windows (4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase), the kidney and dehydration warning, the label's mechanism lines and the gastric emptying wording are all correct.

**Not opened:** three figures came from the label but I didn't open the sentence that holds them. They match the channel's verified figures and my knowledge of the sources:
- the overall hair-loss figure (5.4% vs 0.9%)
- the 4.3–7.1% vs 2.6% stop rates and the 85–91% vs 35% figures from SURMOUNT-1
- the quote in s21, a well-known line from the SURMOUNT-1 abstract

The Mounjaro label and instructions-for-use PDFs load, but their text couldn't be extracted. So the "rotate your injection site" wording in s65 is a paraphrase I couldn't confirm against the page.

**Safety:** all the required lines are there: the pancreatitis and allergy emergency lines with "right away", help numbers for all four countries, the "don't stop or change" line, the kidney caveat on protein, the clinician check before strength training, the low blood sugar caveat, and the prescriber close. Dana is clearly labelled as imaginary.

**Fixes before render:** four small wording fixes (minor), listed below.

issues.claim: The SURMOUNT-1 paper said something similar.
issues.problem: Our craft notes ban 'similar' as a comparison word. The paper's sentence is close to the label's but not the same claim.
issues.fix: The SURMOUNT-1 paper points the same way. The most common side effects were stomach-related, mostly mild to moderate, and they happened primarily during dose escalation.

issues.claim: So a queasy few days after a step up fits the pattern the trials saw.
issues.problem: Neither source gives 'a few days' as a timeframe. The trials only say 'mostly during dose escalation'.
issues.fix: So feeling queasy after a step up fits the pattern the trials saw. It doesn't automatically mean something's wrong, but it's worth mentioning to your prescriber.

issues.problem: A muted viewer doesn't see where this comes from (Zepbound label trials) or the 'mostly during dose escalation' wording.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are legible and don't give away the answer or mismatch emotion/text. #0 ('WHAT CHANGES NEXT?') is clear but generic — it could be the thumbnail for almost any GLP-1 timeline video, so it doesn't stand out in a crowded feed. #2 ('STILL QUEASY?') is emotionally strong and the before/after stomach is a nice visual hook, but the grey-to-red color shift subtly implies a change in state (worse, not better) which slightly narrows the curiosity gap, and the layout is a familiar before/after trope. #1 ('MONTH 2+') wins because it immediately self-selects the exact audience (people past month one wondering what's next), pairs a specific, concrete number with a worried calendar face and a directional arrow that creates urgency, and keeps the actual answer ('what shifts now') completely withheld. Its only minor issue is the smaller secondary line, but the headline number is big and legible enough to carry the click at phone size.

The 9 chapters start at 00:00, cover every section and include the checklist. The description is about 1,140 characters and ends on the exact disclaimer. Hashtags are generic and allowed.
